title: Welcome to Abhi’s Space
text:
Hi, I’m Abhi!
I’m a nature photographer, wildlife enthusiast, birdwatcher and writer.
I love photography, nature, birds, music, and exploring the world around me. This is a space where I document the things I discover, the projects I work on, and the stories I collect along the way.

title: Birdstalking Basics
text:
Well, this first step is pretty easy, and most of us stalkers do it without even thinking. But if you’re unfamiliar with the procedure, allow me to educate you before you embarrass yourself.
First, set your alarm for 5 AM, because birds have unanimously agreed that the most inconvenient hour of the day is the best time to socialise. When it goes off, wake up with your eyelids still glued shut and immediately walk into at least one wall in the dark. This isn’t optional. It’s a compulsory good-luck ritual passed down through generations, or perhaps just something clumsy people like me have turned into a tradition.
Once you’ve recovered from your self-inflicted head trauma, try brushing your teeth while checking for birds outside the window. Then drink a glass of water while checking for birds again. Then change into something vaguely “bird-appropriate” while, you guessed it, checking for birds. At this point, you haven’t even stepped outside, and you’re already behaving like a maniac.
And since we’re already off topic, here’s a discovery from my three long, deeply scientific years in this field: not brushing your teeth seems to increase the number of bird sightings. I have absolutely no explanation for this. Perhaps the universe rewards a combination of chaos and bad breath, but mind you, only if you get the proportions right. The relationship is suspicious enough to deserve a mention.
Now, back to the actual business of stalking birds.
The first thing you need to do is grab your binoculars, your long-lens camera, your overweight field guide, and whatever fancy app you downloaded because the internet told you to. Hold them all in your hands. Feel their weight. Then confidently toss the entire pile into the nearest bin, along with those “identification skills” you definitely never had in the first place.
You don’t need any of these. Remember, we’re stalking birds, and the greatest tool of any stalker is the ability to remain hidden.
Congratulations! You are now ready to step out of your room and not see a single bird anywhere within a five-to-ten-kilometre radius.
It’s an important milestone in the bird-stalking lifestyle. Your first walk outside, and all hope is immediately crushed by the realisation that every bird in the vicinity has apparently decided to go on holiday, a development that eBird has conveniently failed to notify you about.
The most important part of the art, birdwatchers will tell you, is patience.
WRONG!
It’s pure luck and chance. Anyone who claims otherwise is either lying, trying to sound wise, or is a birdwatcher. Birds don’t reward patience. No, they reward an eighteen-sided dice roll in which exactly one face gives you a mere chance of a sighting, while the other seventeen offer disappointment, head-scratching, and existential questions about your life choices.
Now, let’s say it’s your lucky day and you’ve rolled that one magical face. You’ve got a possible sighting. What do you do?
First, shut your mouth. In fact, tape it shut for safety, using a minimum of fifty layers of tape. Birds, unfortunately, do not appreciate the sounds “ahhhh” or “ooohhhh” that humans tend to make when they’re excited. Apparently, they find our enthusiasm deeply offensive.
Finally, in all seriousness, watch them.
And since you’re clearly new to the whole business, let me tell you what you’re supposed to observe, so you don’t end up standing there staring at a bird like a decorative rock.
If you actually want birds to stay long enough for you to watch them, you need to master the ancient art of not behaving like a donkey on a skateboard.
The first rule is simple: move slowly.
And I don’t mean “I’m on a Sunday stroll through the park, questioning my life choices” slowly. I mean slowly enough that, by the end of the year, you’ve managed to move an inch or two at most. Sudden movements make birds assume you’re a predator or, worse, an uncoordinated teenager. So keep everything smooth and deliberate.
When walking, pretend the ground will explode if you stomp too hard. Not because it actually will, but because birds have absolutely zero tolerance for dramatic humans crashing through piles of leaves.
One particularly important skill I’ve picked up over the years is to step on rocks wherever possible rather than mud or leaf litter. Rocks are less likely to harbour hidden saboteurs such as dry leaves and twigs that betray your presence with a single unfortunate crunch. Through years of rigorous, highly scientific stalking research, I’ve also discovered that plants are considerably less likely to grow on rocks than on mud. This means fewer thorny surprises for barefoot stalkers such as myself.
You may complain that your feet hurt from walking barefoot, but complaining is a privilege reserved for birdwatchers. Real stalkers accept discomfort and pain as the price of invisibility and success. Or at least that’s what I tell myself when I step on something particularly unpleasant.
Sound is another important aspect of bird stalking. A soft cough can ruin everything, so if you feel one coming, swallow it as if it were your pride after that one particularly disastrous maths exam. In fact, anything louder than a polite sneeze is apparently reasonable grounds for immediate evacuation.
The goal is to blend into the background so well that even you begin questioning whether you exist.
Then there’s positioning and location. Most people assume that standing directly in front of a bird gives them the best view. Sure, if your goal is to scare it away instantly. The trick is to observe from an angle, preferably with some form of cover, such as trees, rocks or bushes. Birds appreciate it when you respect their personal-space bubble. Staying partly hidden also makes you look less like a threat and more like a particularly confused shrub.
As a general rule of thumb, if you can’t see the bird, the bird probably can’t see you either.
So, let’s say you know there’s a bird sitting in a tree about fifteen metres away. What do you do? You immediately try to lose sight of it.
This may sound confusing, and probably looks like a rather questionable thing to do, but that’s essentially bird stalking. Since you already know where the bird is, your next objective is to get close enough to regain sight of it, this time from a shorter distance.
Keep in mind, however, that the rule “If you can’t see the bird, the bird can’t see you” applies only to your sense of sight. Unfortunately, birds are equipped with other senses too. They can hear you, and, strangely and rather worryingly, sometimes they just seem to know you’re there.
And that’s the end of your first lesson.
Congratulations, hatchling stalker! You’ve survived the early-morning alarm trauma, perfected the art of walking like a confused shrub, mastered the technique of stepping on rocks to avoid thorns, and discovered that birds are suspicious little geniuses who hear everything and sometimes just know.
Remember the basics: wake up at absurd hours, move slowly enough to challenge the sloth’s world record, respect their personal-space bubbles, and keep your mouth taped shut if necessary.
Above all, remember that you’re not here to disturb the birds. You’re here to spend several hours watching them do absolutely nothing, only to return home with one blurry photograph and the satisfaction of having successfully ruined your sleep schedule.
Good Luck on your adventure!!!
